summary: This memo describes the administrative model for SNMPv2, which defines how the administrative framework applies to network management across different configurations and environments, using parties, contexts, and access control. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This paper sets the rules for who can ask what of a network device. It is historic and later versions of SNMP used a different approach.

questions: what is a mib view in snmp
subtitle: Security and access control framework for SNMPv2 network management.

tldr.problem: SNMPv1 used a community-based model that offered weak security and poor access control. As SNMP became critical for managing production networks, a better framework was needed to authenticate management stations, protect message integrity, encrypt sensitive data, and enforce granular access policies.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1445 introduces SNMPv2 parties (identified entities), contexts (collections of managed objects), and authentication and privacy protocols. Each party has an identity, authentication method, and privacy settings. Access control policies determine what objects each party can read or modify. Proxy relationships allow management of remote devices transparently.
tldr.outcome: This administrative model became the foundation for SNMPv2, enabling secure network management with proper access control. However, it is now historic; SNMPv3 (RFC 3412) later replaced this party-based model with user-based security that proved more flexible and is the modern standard.

today: RFC 1445 is Historic. RFC 3412 (SNMPv3) introduced a user-based security model that replaced the party-based model, and SNMPv3 is now the recommended version for all new SNMP deployments.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Network management systems monitor and control devices across the Internet through a network management protocol. These systems need to identify which management station is sending a request, verify it is authentic, protect sensitive data from eavesdropping, and enforce policies about what each station can access.

SNMPv1 (the original Simple Network Management Protocol) used a community-string-based model: a shared secret string authenticated all requests from a management station. This was weak because the community string offered only limited protection against unauthorized access, provided no privacy protection, and could not distinguish between different management stations sharing the same string.

RFC 1445 defines the administrative model for SNMPv2, introducing a more sophisticated framework based on identities, authentication protocols, privacy protocols, and access control policies. This model shifts from shared secrets to identified parties with explicit security bindings.
sections.eli5: Before, network management used a password everyone shared. The new way gives each tool an identity, proves it is real, hides the secrets it sends, and says exactly what it is allowed to do.

sections.title: Parties, Entities, and Contexts
sections.content:
A SNMPv2 party is a virtual entity representing a management principal (typically a management station or agent) that operates under a specific set of security rules. Each party has four key components: a unique identity, a transport address where it can be reached, authentication credentials (a protocol and keys), and privacy credentials (an encryption method and keys).

A SNMPv2 entity is the actual software process that generates and responds to SNMPv2 messages. An entity can act as multiple parties, each with different security bindings and access permissions. This separates the logical identity (party) from the implementation (entity).

A SNMPv2 context is a collection of managed objects that a party can access. For local objects (like those on an agent device), the context defines a MIB view—a subset of the agent's managed objects. For remote objects, the context defines a proxy relationship where one agent forwards requests to another. A management communication specifies a source party, destination party, context, and the protocol operation (get, set, etc.).
sections.eli5: A party is like a person with a name and a password. An entity is the actual computer. A context is a set of things that party can see. Each message says who is asking, who they are asking, what things they want to see, and what they want to do.

sections.title: Authentication and Privacy
sections.content:
SNMPv2 management communications can be protected in two optional layers. Authentication verifies the identity of the sender and protects message integrity using a protocol and secret key. Privacy encrypts the message contents so eavesdroppers cannot read sensitive data like community strings or configuration values.

Each party specifies its authentication protocol (or "noAuth" for no authentication) and its privacy protocol (or "noPriv" for no encryption). An entity acting as a non-secure party (both noAuth and noPriv) operates like SNMPv1. Secure parties use cryptographic protection.

Authentication information is included in the message header, allowing the receiving party to verify the message came from the claimed source. Privacy data is encrypted and must be decrypted using the privacy key. The architecture supports plugging in different authentication and privacy algorithms, allowing implementations to upgrade cryptographic methods as better algorithms become available.
sections.eli5: Messages can be checked to prove they are really from the right place and that nobody changed them. Messages can also be scrambled so only the right person can read them. Neither is required, but both can be turned on.

sections.title: Access Control and MIB Views
sections.content:
Access control in SNMPv2 is enforced through access control policies that specify what each party can do. A party can be granted permission to read certain managed objects, write to certain objects, send specific PDU types (like get or set), or perform proxy operations.

Access is scoped by MIB view—a subset of the managed object identifier tree. A view subtree is identified by an object identifier prefix; all objects with that prefix belong to the view. By assigning parties to specific views, an administrator can prevent management stations from accessing sensitive information. For example, a monitoring station might read performance metrics but not configuration parameters, while a privileged management system might modify both.

This view-based access control is granular enough for most deployments but allows instance-level granularity where needed. Configuration of views and policies happens through the agent's configuration files or management interfaces, not through the protocol itself.
sections.eli5: Each party gets a list of what it is allowed to see and change. If a party tries to look at something it is not allowed to, the answer is no.
